attribution.note: Marcus's own words on his own blog. He repeats his bet offer against Musk's forecast. The quote of Musk is used only to identify what the bet is against.

semantics.note: Standing by a million-dollar bet is a firm, unhedged commitment against Musk's one-to-two-year forecast. The 'possibly' hedge is Musk's, not Marcus's. The added bet clause is not checkable, and the contract correctly leaves it ungraded.

contract.note: Taking the latest reasonable end of 'a year or two' (2026-10-30) is generous to the speaker and ordinary. Counting physical tasks as part of 'anything any human can do' is the plain reading. The early-contradiction rule is reasonable.

evidence.note: Fortune report confirming Musk's 2024-10-29 forecast, which the bet targets. It shows what the claim is about, not how it turned out.

CAIS reports a best Remote Labor Index (RLI) automation rate of 15.8% as of July 2026. It shows no AI at human level on all tasks, so the early-contradiction rule is not met. But it predates the deadline, so it cannot support the claim.

reviews.rationale: The deadline is 2026-10-30, after the evaluation date of 2026-10-28. The rule for early contradiction is not met: the July 2026 RLI data show AI completing only 15.8% of remote projects, far from doing anything a human can do. Support can only come after the deadline, so the claim stays unresolved for now.

attribution.note: Marcus quotes his own comment to Decrypt on his own blog, so the words are his and endorsed.

semantics.note: 'Just fantasy' is firm, unhedged language. The 200x Roomba threshold (about 10 billion units) and the 'nearish term' horizon are kept.

contract.note: Deriving 10 billion cumulative units from 200 x 50 million is ordinary arithmetic. Treating 'nearish term' as having no endpoint is fair. Marking the contract retrospective is a small labelling slip and does not affect the result.

evidence.note: Omdia estimates about 13,318 shipments in 2025, counting wheeled embodied robots too. These are annual shipments, not cumulative humanoid sales. The figure is far below the threshold but cannot support the claim before an endpoint.

reviews.rationale: 'Nearish term' sets no deadline. The contract allows only early contradiction, by verified sales near 10 billion, and the evidence shows about 13,000 units shipped in 2025, nowhere near that. Low sales before an unstated endpoint cannot establish support, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus quotes his own comment to Decrypt on his own blog, so the words are his and endorsed.

semantics.note: A present-tense factual claim about the state of humanoid engineering in October 2024. 'At any price' is correctly kept as a qualifier, not a condition.

contract.note: The result depends on how 'generally useful', 'safe' and 'reliable' are read, and the speaker set no thresholds. The contract's reading is ordinary: broad, dependable, autonomous operation, not perfection. Reading 'nobody knows' as 'no demonstrated capability' is not stretched either way.

evidence.note: IEEE Transmitter, 2024-10-24: humanoids are still in development, simple tasks need heavy training, and they work best in controlled, repetitive settings. Contemporaneous and from outside the industry.
Boston Dynamics/TRI press release, 2024-10-16. It presents general-purpose humanoids as a goal still being developed. It is a company disclosure and covers only Atlas, so it is weak corroboration.
Agility's 2024-10-03 marketing post on Digit's GXO deployment. It describes Digit as built to 'do many things' but offers no validation of broad, safe, reliable performance.

BMW's August 2024 release on a Figure 02 trial. It predates the target period and the capability claims are Figure's own. It also says no Figure robots were at the plant, so it is not broad validation.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract's fair, ordinary reading, contemporaneous expert reporting (e1) describes humanoids as still in development, working best on narrow, repetitive tasks in controlled settings. Boston Dynamics (e2) frames general-purpose humanoids as a goal. The counterevidence (e3, e4) is company marketing or a single narrow trial with no validation of broad, safe, reliable autonomy. The October 2024 observation is supported.

attribution.note: Marcus quotes his own comment to Decrypt on his own blog, so the words are his and endorsed.

semantics.note: 'Will be true' and 'aren't going to see' are firm language. The proposition rightly folds in the affordability/need clause carried by 'the same'. 'Anytime soon' is kept as an open horizon.

contract.note: Reading 'cars' as cars in use and asking for a worldwide stock ratio is ordinary. Separating the affordability part from the ratio part is fair. Marking it retrospective is a small labelling slip.

evidence.note: Altman Solon survey of US consumers, November 2025, on home robots in general. It finds price resistance but also 65% interest. It covers stated preferences in one country only, so it settles neither global affordability nor the six-to-one stock ratio.

reviews.rationale: 'Anytime soon' sets no deadline. Nothing in the packet shows a six-to-one humanoid-to-car stock ratio, so there is no early contradiction. The only evidence is a US survey of stated preferences, which mixes price resistance with strong interest, so it cannot settle the affordability part. Under the contract, no support is possible before an endpoint, so the claim is unresolved.
